rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: Determine how sick the patient looks.
rationale.Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular: Cardiac pathology could cause leg pain — cardiovascular exam essential.
rationale.Physical Exam: Extremities / Spine: Chief complaint — examine extremities for pulses, skin changes, temperature.
rationale.Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych: Neurological issues on differential for leg pain — neuro exam needed.
rationale.ECG, 12 lead: Rule out cardiac causes of leg pain. PAD patients often have concomitant CAD.
rationale.Hemoglobin A1C, blood: All patients with possible PVD should be evaluated for diabetes.
rationale.Lipid profile: Lipids contribute to atherosclerosis — check and treat if abnormal. Goal LDL < 100 in PAD.
rationale.Microalbumin, urine (24-hour or spot): Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes — screen for early glomerular disease.
rationale.Ankle-brachial index / Arterial Doppler,: ABI is the main diagnostic tool. ABI < 0.7 = claudication. Normal ≥ 1.0. Non-invasive, first-line.
rationale.Angiography, lower extremity: Invasive test with contrast risks. Conservative management first for intermittent claudication, not rest pain.
rationale.Metformin: First-line therapy for type 2 diabetes. Start at diagnosis.
rationale.ACE inhibitor (Lisinopril / Enalapril /: ACE inhibitors are first-line for hypertensive diabetics — nephroprotective. ARB if ACEI intolerant.
rationale.Statin (Atorvastatin / Rosuvastatin / Si: Statin for hyperlipidemia — prevents worsening of PVD. Goal LDL < 100 mg/dL.
rationale.Aspirin, therapy: Antiplatelet therapy indicated for PAD. Aspirin is most common and most tested. Reduces cardiovascular events.
rationale.Instruct patient, smoking cessation: One of the most important interventions — smoking accelerates PVD.
rationale.Diet modification (calorie-restricted /: Weight loss to control diabetes and hypertension. DASH diet for hypertension.
rationale.Instruct patient, diabetes: Diabetes education increases compliance and improves outcomes.
rationale.Advise patient, exercise program: Exercise is excellent for weight loss, glucose control, and collateral circulation development. Supervised walking programs improve claudication symptoms.
rationale.Angiography / Arteriography: Invasive, uses contrast (nephrotoxic, allergic reactions), expensive. Conservative management with risk factor modification is first-line for intermittent claudication. Only for rest pain or failed medical therapy.
rationale.Surgical bypass / Angioplasty: Not indicated for intermittent claudication. Reserved for rest pain, tissue loss, or disabling symptoms refractory to conservative therapy.
rationale.CT angiography: Radiation + iodinated contrast exposure. Duplex ultrasound or ABI is preferred non-invasive screening.

hpi: {{patient_name}} is a middle-aged man with multiple cardiovascular risk factors — hypertension, hyperlipidemia, newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, and smoking — who presents with bilateral leg pain on exertion that is relieved by rest (intermittent claudication). He has diminished peripheral pulses and cool extremities. The ankle-brachial index is less than 0.7, consistent with moderate PAD (normal ≥ 1.0, claudication < 0.7, rest pain < 0.4). Importantly, he has intermittent claudication rather than rest pain, which means conservative management is appropriate rather than invasive intervention. The 6 P's of peripheral artery disease are: Pulselessness, Pain, Pallor, Poikilothermia, Paresthesia, and Paralysis.

physical_exam: Diminished peripheral pulses. Assess for bruits (carotid, femoral). Hypertension.

Rule out neurogenic claudication (spinal stenosis) vs vascular claudication. Vascular: pain with exertion, relieved quickly by rest. Neurogenic: pain with standing/walking, relieved by sitting/leaning forward.

chief_complaint: Bilateral leg pain on exertion, relieved by rest
case_summary: PAD with intermittent claudication. Multiple risk factors: HTN, HLD, DM2, smoking. ABI < 0.7 confirms. Conservative management: aspirin, statin, ACEI, metformin, smoking cessation, diet, exercise. Avoid invasive angiography. Follow-up in 7 days. Prognosis: good with risk factor control.
